data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms as a 'critical preference' grounded in the logic of testing rather than induction, but accepting this costs the agent any rational assurance that the preferred theory will succeed in the future or approximate truth more closely than its rivals.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If corroboration is shown to logically entail a prediction of future success (even probabilistic), the distinction collapses into induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper cannot explain why acting on a less-corroborated theory is irrational without invoking the principle that past performance indicates future reliability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'cost' of no assurance renders the preference practically indistinguishable from random choice for decision-makers requiring risk assessment.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'inductive inference' (claiming past success raises future probability) and 'critical preference' (choosing the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification as the best available target for further criticism and action). Preference is justified not by expected utility derived from probability, but by the methodological rule that acting on the most severely tested theory maximizes the potential for learning if the theory fails, and represents the current state of critical discussion if it holds. The preference is a decision to treat the unrefuted, high-content theory as the provisional basis for action because it is the only one that has survived the specific risks designed to kill it.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
